title: Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic to be named AI national champions, WSJ reports
content:
The Trump administration plans to name Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic among more than two dozen AI “national champions”, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday. The aim is to help US AI firms win business overseas against Chinese rivals.
People familiar with the plans told Yoko Kubota and Amrith Ramkumar that the announcement could come within the next week. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick would unveil the list of AI national champions, the Journal reported. The timing could still change.
A package deal for foreign buyers
The programme aims to persuade foreign governments and companies to choose US AI over Chinese technology. It would bundle American chips, AI models and other products into packages that are easier for overseas customers to buy, according to the Journal.
Commerce already runs the American AI Exports Program. A July 2025 executive order set it up to sell full packages of US AI abroad. In July this year, the department said groups of companies had filed 78 applications. Packages it designates may get government advocacy, federal financing and faster export licence reviews, it said.
China is pushing its own AI abroad too. In October, Chinese state media said Beijing had cleared DeepSeek and MiniMax to take their models overseas.
Nvidia under scrutiny
The plan shows the administration pressing ahead with its tech strategy despite the turmoil at Nvidia, the Journal reported. Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on Thursday. He had admitted an affair with Alice Huang, whom US officials suspect of spying for China.
The revelations have added to pressure from critics who want national security put ahead of market share, the Journal reported. Some fear Chinese companies are getting top Nvidia chips through gaps in export controls.
Trump has repeatedly praised Nvidia and Huang. In October he gave Huang the National Medal of Science.
Critics have accused Lutnick’s Commerce Department of failing to close those gaps, the Journal reported. It had previously reported that he was wary of angering Beijing during trade talks. Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Commerce “has the pen” on blacklisting Megaspeed. The Singapore firm sits at the centre of the Nvidia case.
The list would land in the week Trump travels to China. He attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November. He plans to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping there.

report.summary: Trump administration plans to name Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, OpenAI, Anthropic and others as AI 'national champions' to boost US AI exports against China.
report.background: The move comes amid intensifying US-China competition over AI hardware and models. The Commerce Department already runs the American AI Exports Program, set up by a July 2025 executive order to sell bundled US AI packages abroad. By July this year, 78 applications had been filed by company groups. China is also pushing its AI overseas: in October, state media said Beijing cleared DeepSeek and MiniMax to expand internationally. The national champions list would formalize government backing for selected US firms. It lands amid turmoil at Nvidia, where CEO Jensen Huang reportedly resigned after admitting an affair with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China. Critics worry export control gaps let Chinese firms obtain top Nvidia chips. The announcement could coincide with Trump's Asia-Pacific trip to Shenzhen on 18-19 November, where he plans to meet Xi Jinping.
key_points: The Trump administration plans to designate more than two dozen AI 'national champions', including Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is expected to unveil the list, possibly within the next week, though timing could change.

The programme bundles American chips, AI models and other products into packages that foreign governments and companies can buy more easily. Designated packages may receive government advocacy, federal financing and faster export licence reviews under the existing American AI Exports Program.

The goal is to persuade overseas buyers to choose US AI over Chinese technology. China is pushing its own AI abroad too; in October, state media said Beijing had cleared DeepSeek and MiniMax to take their models overseas.

The plan proceeds despite turmoil at Nvidia. CEO Jensen Huang resigned after admitting an affair with Alice Huang, whom US officials suspect of spying for China. Critics want national security prioritised over market share and fear Chinese firms are getting top Nvidia chips through export control gaps.
The list could land the same week Trump travels to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, where he plans to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the list formalises state-backed export promotion, potentially entrenching US vendors in foreign markets and raising pressure on Chinese rivals. Developers may see more bundled hardware-model offerings and government financing, but also tighter alignment with US policy. Regular users abroad could gain easier access to US AI tools, though geopolitical lock-in may limit choice. The Nvidia turmoil and export-control concerns add risk: critics argue commercial interests may overshadow national security, while Nvidia's leadership shake-up could complicate the programme's rollout. The timing near Trump-Xi talks signals AI is now a top-tier diplomatic lever, not just a commercial sector.
report.tools: Follow the Commerce Department's American AI Exports Program for official updates. Track export control changes via the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS). Compare Chinese open models DeepSeek and MiniMax with US open-weight alternatives like Llama and Mistral. Policy trackers from CSIS and Stanford HAI offer context on AI export competition.
